content_voiceover: This is a nice visual summary of Langerhans cell histiocytosis and where it shows up in the body. The disease is an excess of immature Langerhans cells, which are antigen presenting immune cells normally found in the skin, forming granulomas across multiple organs. About fifty percent of cases carry a somatic B R A F mutation, prevalence is roughly one to two per one hundred thousand, with a two to one male to female ratio, and it's most commonly diagnosed in children age one to three. Clinically, children tend to present with acute disseminated multisystem disease, while adults and older children more often have indolent single organ disease. Going organ by organ: bone granulomas are the most common finding at seventy seven percent, typically in the skull and long bones, causing pain, swelling, and fractures, and you'll often see a classic punched out lytic skull lesion on X ray. Skin and mucosal granulomas occur in thirty nine percent, presenting as blisters, papules, or a maculopapular rash, classically a scaly eczematous diaper rash that's refractory to standard treatment. Lymph node and bone marrow granulomas occur in nineteen percent, causing lymphadenopathy and pancytopenia. CNS and pituitary granulomas occur in only six percent but are high yield for boards, causing headache, dizziness, proptosis, seizures, and critically diabetes insipidus from loss of A D H, plus growth hormone loss, pubertal delay from G n R H deficiency, and hypothyroidism from T S H loss. Lung granulomas occur in ten percent, more common in adult smokers, causing respiratory distress, pneumothorax, chronic cough, and weight loss. Liver granulomas occur in sixteen percent with jaundice, elevated transaminases, ascites, hypoalbuminemia, and factor deficiencies, and splenic granulomas occur in thirteen percent causing splenomegaly. Diagnosis is by biopsy of the granuloma with immunohistochemical staining and electron microscopy, and treatment includes prednisone, vinblastine, curettage of bone lesions, and topical therapy for skin disease.
keypoints: Bone involvement is most common (77%): skull and long bones, classic punched-out lytic lesions
Diabetes insipidus from CNS/pituitary involvement (6%) is a high-yield board finding, along with growth hormone and TSH loss
Classic infant presentation: scaly, eczematous diaper rash refractory to standard treatment
Diagnosis: biopsy with IHC and electron microscopy; treatment: prednisone, vinblastine, curettage, topical therapy
